claim: Low complexity regions (LCRs) play a role in a variety of important biological processes.
source: Low complexity regions (LCRs) play a role in a variety of important biological processes, yet we lack a unified view of their sequences, features, relationships, and functions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the motivation for the study. It is supported by the broader literature context implied by the manuscript.

claim: LCR type and copy number contribute to higher order assemblies.
source: By defining LCR relationships across the proteome, we provide insight into how LCR type and copy number contribute to higher order assemblies, such as the importance of K-rich LCR copy number for assembly of the nucleolar protein RPA43 in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing that RPA43 requires at least 2 K-rich LCRs for nucleolar localization and phase separation.

claim: K-rich LCR copy number is important for assembly of the nucleolar protein RPA43 in vivo and in vitro.
source: By defining LCR relationships across the proteome, we provide insight into how LCR type and copy number contribute to higher order assemblies, such as the importance of K-rich LCR copy number for assembly of the nucleolar protein RPA43 in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Experimental data in Figure 2D and 2E demonstrate that RPA43 mutants with two K-rich LCRs localize to the nucleolus and phase separate in vitro, while those with one or zero do not.

claim: LCR maps reveal the underlying structure of LCR sequence space.
source: With LCR maps, we reveal the underlying structure of LCR sequence space, and relate differential occupancy in this space to the conservation and emergence of higher order assemblies, including the metazoan extracellular matrix and plant cell wall.
evidence: The manuscript presents UMAP visualizations (Figure 3A, Figure 5A) that show the distribution of LCRs in sequence space.

claim: Differential occupancy in LCR sequence space relates to the conservation and emergence of higher order assemblies, including the metazoan extracellular matrix and plant cell wall.
source: With LCR maps, we reveal the underlying structure of LCR sequence space, and relate differential occupancy in this space to the conservation and emergence of higher order assemblies, including the metazoan extracellular matrix and plant cell wall.
evidence: The manuscript shows that ECM proteins occupy the G/P cluster primarily in metazoans (Figure 5C), and plant cell wall proteins occupy distinct P-rich regions (Figure 5D).

claim: LCR relationships and maps uncover scaffold-client relationships among E-rich LCR-containing proteins in the nucleolus.
source: Together, LCR relationships and maps uncover and identify scaffold-client relationships among E-rich LCR-containing proteins in the nucleolus, and revealed previously undescribed regions of LCR sequence space with signatures of higher order assemblies, including a teleost-specific T/H-rich sequence space.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates that TCOF, with many E-rich LCRs, acts as a scaffold that recruits RPA1 and UBF1, which have fewer E-rich LCRs (Figure 4F, 4G).

claim: There exist previously undescribed regions of LCR sequence space with signatures of higher order assemblies, including a teleost-specific T/H-rich sequence space.
source: Together, LCR relationships and maps uncover and identify scaffold-client relationships among E-rich LCR-containing proteins in the nucleolus, and revealed previously undescribed regions of LCR sequence space with signatures of higher order assemblies, including a teleost-specific T/H-rich sequence space.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a T/H-rich cluster specific to teleost fish (Figure 6A, 6D) with proteins containing multiple T/H-rich LCRs.

claim: Low complexity regions are abundant in proteomes.
source: Low complexity regions (LCRs) of proteins, sequences that frequently repeat the same amino acids (e.g. 'AAAAAAA' or 'LLQLLLSLL'), are abundant in proteomes (DePristo et al., 2006; Huntley and Clark, 2007; Haerty and Golding, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LCRs are found in proteins which play a role in many different biological processes such as transcription, stress response, and extracellular structure.
source: These contiguous regions of low sequence entropy are found in proteins which play a role in many different biological processes such as transcription, stress response, and extracellular structure (Coletta et al., 2010; Cascarina and Ross, 2018; Mier et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some LCR-containing proteins direct the higher order assembly of intracellular membraneless bodies.
source: More recently, some LCR-containing proteins have been shown to direct the higher order assembly of intracellular membraneless bodies (Patel et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Specific residues are required for the intermolecular interactions responsible for higher order assembly in some LCRs.
source: Experimental approaches, such as NMR and SAXS, have found examples where specific residues are required for the intermolecular interactions responsible for higher order assembly (Kim et al., 2019b; Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Computational identification of short linear motifs (SLiMs) have cataloged specific sub-sequences in LCRs which mediate certain interactions and post-translational modifications.
source: Computational identification of short linear motifs (SLiMs) have cataloged specific sub-sequences in LCRs which mediate certain interactions and post-translational modifications (Krystkowiak and Davey, 2017; Kumar et al., 2020), and biophysical predictions of LCRs have given insight into how certain physical properties may direct self-assembly of large compartments (Das and Pappu, 2013; Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Biophysical predictions of LCRs have given insight into how certain physical properties may direct self-assembly of large compartments.
source: Computational identification of short linear motifs (SLiMs) have cataloged specific sub-sequences in LCRs which mediate certain interactions and post-translational modifications (Krystkowiak and Davey, 2017; Kumar et al., 2020), and biophysical predictions of LCRs have given insight into how certain physical properties may direct self-assembly of large compartments (Das and Pappu, 2013; Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Valency facilitates the formation of higher order assemblies through interactions between multivalent scaffold proteins, which recruit low-valency clients.
source: Valency, defined by the number of binding sites in a molecule, facilitates the formation of higher order assemblies through interactions between multivalent scaffold proteins, which recruit low-valency clients (Banani et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Valency can be encoded in any type of sequence.
source: Valency can be encoded in any type of sequence (Li et al., 2012; Banani et al., 2016; Banani et al., 2017), yet it has only been studied in a few LCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The contributions of individual LCRs on protein function can depend on their identities in proteins with multiple LCRs.
source: Recent work has shown that in proteins with multiple LCRs, the contributions of individual LCRs on protein function can depend on their identities (Hebert and Matera, 2000; Mitrea et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Multiple copies of the same LCR can increase the valency of a protein in synthetic systems.
source: Synthetic systems have shown that multiple copies of the same LCR can increase the valency of a protein (Schuster et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Structural assemblies such as the extracellular matrix, spider silk, and the siliceous skeleton of certain sponges are comprised of proteins which share features with proteins involved in intracellular assemblies.
source: More broadly, the importance of LCR features and relationships discussed above is not restricted to proteins of intracellular higher order assemblies. Structural assemblies such as the extracellular matrix (Forgacs et al., 2003; Rauscher and Pomès, 2017), spider silk (Xu and Lewis, 1990; Hinman and Lewis, 1992; Malay, 2020), and the siliceous skeleton of certain sponges (Shimizu et al., 2015) are comprised of proteins which share features with proteins involved in intracellular assemblies, such as multivalent scaffolding proteins abundant in LCRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many of the proteins comprising extracellular assemblies are composed almost entirely of LCRs which are known to mediate multivalent interactions.
source: In fact, many of the proteins comprising these assemblies are composed almost entirely of LCRs which are known to mediate multivalent interactions (Rauscher et al., 2006; Malay, 2020), suggesting that the contribution of LCRs to valency and hierarchical assembly also play a role in these diverse extracellular assemblies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dotplots can identify LCRs in proteins and reveal the relationships between similar and distinct LCRs for proteins with multiple LCRs.
source: Therefore, dotplots are capable of identifying LCRs in proteins and revealing the relationships between similar and distinct LCRs for proteins with multiple LCRs.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates this capability through examples like G3BP1 (Figure 1A) where dotplots distinguish between different LCR types.

claim: G3BP1 has LCR relationships where two LCRs are similar to each other (LCR1 and 2) and distinct from a third LCR (LCR3).
source: The dotplot reveals that G3BP1 has LCR relationships where two LCRs are similar to each other (LCR1 and 2) and distinct from a third LCR (LCR3).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A where the dotplot pattern reveals these relationships.

claim: The presence of compositionally distinct LCRs in G3BP1 are critical for the ability of G3BP1 to form stress granules.
source: Previous studies have shown that the presence of these compositionally distinct LCRs are critical for the ability of G3BP1 to form stress granules (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The acidic LCRs (LCR1 and 2) of G3BP1 interact with and inhibit the RGG domain (containing LCR3).
source: The acidic LCRs (LCR1 and 2 in Figure 1A) interact with and inhibit the RGG domain (containing LCR3 in Figure 1A) which plays a role in RNA-binding (Kim et al., 2019a), a necessary step of stress granule assembly (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SRRM2 and SON act as essential scaffolds for formation of nuclear speckles.
source: SRRM2 and another LCR-containing protein SON (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) were recently found to act as essential scaffolds for formation of nuclear speckles (Sharma et al., 2010; Fei et al., 2017; Ilik et al., 2020), suggesting that proteins which each contain long stretches of similar LCR sequences could play important roles in certain higher order assemblies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: UBP2L and PRC2C are essential for the formation of stress granules.
source: These include UBP2L and PRC2C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G), which were only recently discovered to be essential for the formation of stress granules (Youn et al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mucins are key components of mucus, a liquid/gel-like assembly of glycoproteins.
source: Mucins are key components of mucus, a liquid/gel-like assembly of glycoproteins (reviewed in Lai et al., 2009), while DSPP codes for a protein which scaffolds the mineralization of teeth (Stetler-Stevenson and Veis, 1986; Saito et al., 2000; Sreenath et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DSPP codes for a protein which scaffolds the mineralization of teeth.
source: Mucins are key components of mucus, a liquid/gel-like assembly of glycoproteins (reviewed in Lai et al., 2009), while DSPP codes for a protein which scaffolds the mineralization of teeth (Stetler-Stevenson and Veis, 1986; Saito et al., 2000; Sreenath et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dotplot approach identified 37,342 LCRs in 14,156 proteins in the human proteome.
source: Across the human proteome, our approach identified 37,342 LCRs in 14,156 proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), with nearly 60% of LCR-containing proteins in the human proteome containing more than one LCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a direct result from applying the computational pipeline to the human proteome.

claim: Nearly 60% of LCR-containing proteins in the human proteome contain more than one LCR.
source: Across the human proteome, our approach identified 37,342 LCRs in 14,156 proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), with nearly 60% of LCR-containing proteins in the human proteome containing more than one LCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E as a cumulative distribution.

claim: The Shannon entropy of LCRs identified by the dotplot approach is significantly lower than that of randomly sampled sequences from the proteome.
source: The Shannon entropy of these regions was significantly lower than that of randomly sampled sequences from the proteome, confirming that they are low complexity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2D shows cumulative distributions comparing LCR entropy to random sequences.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between the convolved pixel intensity threshold used for segmentation and the resulting Shannon entropy of called LCRs.
source: Furthermore, we observe an inverse relationship between the convolved pixel intensity threshold used for segmentation and the resulting Shannon entropy of called LCRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This relationship is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The density of points in dotplots is inversely related to the informational complexity of the corresponding sequence.
source: The tight relationship between these values shows that, in general, the density of points in dotplots is inversely related to the informational complexity of the corresponding sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverse relationship between convolved pixel intensity and Shannon entropy.

claim: Coilin has 4 distinct types of LCRs, with one of the types present in two copies.
source: For Coilin, we identify 4 distinct types of LCRs, with one of the types present in two copies (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E through the dotplot analysis and graph representation.

claim: Two of the four LCR types in Coilin have been shown to play different roles in Coilin localization to cajal bodies.
source: Of these four types, two of them have been shown to play different roles in Coilin localization to cajal bodies (Hebert and Matera, 2000), showing that our systematic dotplot approach can distinguish LCR types and that these types can have different functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RPA43 has three LCRs in its C-terminus which are all the same type.
source: From our analysis, we found that RPA43 has three LCRs in its C-terminus which are all the same type (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A through dotplot analysis.

claim: All three LCRs of RPA43 contained a 10–12 amino acid block of mostly K-residues.
source: All three LCRs of RPA43 contained a 10–12 amino acid block of mostly K-residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, bottom row), which were the primary contributor to off-diagonal intersections between these LCRs and thus defined this LCR type.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A where the LCR sequences are displayed.

claim: GFP-fused WT RPA43 localized to the fibrillar center of the nucleolus.
source: While GFP-fused WT RPA43 localized correctly to the fibrillar center of the nucleolus, deletion of all three of its K-rich LCRs (ΔK1,2,3) led to its exclusion from the nucleolus, confirming that these LCRs are important for its higher order assembly (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D through immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: Deletion of all three K-rich LCRs of RPA43 (ΔK1,2,3) led to its exclusion from the nucleolus.
source: While GFP-fused WT RPA43 localized correctly to the fibrillar center of the nucleolus, deletion of all three of its K-rich LCRs (ΔK1,2,3) led to its exclusion from the nucleolus, confirming that these LCRs are important for its higher order assembly (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D through immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: RPA43 mutants with two copies of its K-rich LCRs correctly localized to the nucleolus.
source: Surprisingly, RPA43 mutants with two copies of its LCRs correctly localized to the nucleolus, while those containing only one of its LCRs were not (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C through immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: RPA43 mutants containing only one K-rich LCR did not correctly localize to the nucleolus.
source: Surprisingly, RPA43 mutants with two copies of its LCRs correctly localized to the nucleolus, while those containing only one of its LCRs were not (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C through immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: A copy number of at least 2 K-rich LCRs is required for RPA43 integration into the nucleolus.
source: In fact, two of the three double mutants were strongly excluded from the nucleolus, showing that these LCRs do not uniquely contribute to RPA43 localization. Rather, it is a copy number of at least 2 of these LCRs which is required for RPA43 integration into the nucleolus.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that any combination of 2 K-rich LCRs is sufficient for nucleolar localization.

claim: Recombinant GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus phase separated into liquid droplets in vitro.
source: Consistent with these results, while the recombinant GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus phase separated into liquid droplets in vitro, the GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus with its three K-rich LCRs specifically deleted did not (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E through droplet formation assays.

claim: GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus with its three K-rich LCRs deleted did not phase separate in vitro.
source: Consistent with these results, while the recombinant GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus phase separated into liquid droplets in vitro, the GFP-fused RPA43 C-terminus with its three K-rich LCRs specifically deleted did not (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E through droplet formation assays.

claim: The RPA43 C-terminus contains the sequences sufficient for higher order assembly.
source: Thus, the RPA43 C-terminus contains the sequences sufficient for higher order assembly, and the K-rich LCRs are necessary for this assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro phase separation results showing that the C-terminus alone can form droplets.

claim: The K-rich LCRs of RPA43 are necessary for higher order assembly.
source: Thus, the RPA43 C-terminus contains the sequences sufficient for higher order assembly, and the K-rich LCRs are necessary for this assembly.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that deletion of K-rich LCRs abolishes phase separation.

claim: The K-rich LCRs of RPA43 participate in intermolecular interactions.
source: This result suggests that the K-rich LCRs are not merely linkers between other self-interacting elements, as deletion of such linkers tends to alter the physical properties of the assembly but not its presence (Martin et al., 2020). Rather, our results suggest that these K-rich LCRs participate in intermolecular interactions, and that K-rich LCR copy number may more generally contribute to protein valency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of K-rich LCRs completely abolishes assembly rather than just altering its properties.

claim: LCRs in the human proteome exhibit a rich diversity of sequence compositions.
source: This map shows that LCRs in the human proteome exhibit a rich diversity of sequence compositions, and do not fall into a handful of isolated groups.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A where the UMAP reveals continuous distributions of LCRs across sequence space.

claim: 19 clusters of LCRs were identified in the human proteome LCR map using Leiden clustering.
source: Using Leiden clustering (Traag et al., 2019), we identified 19 clusters of LCRs in this space which mostly corresponded to high frequency of an amino acid.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A where clusters are labeled and colored.

claim: Many LCR clusters are connected to other clusters through bridge-like connections.
source: Strikingly, many clusters are 'connected' to other clusters through bridge-like connections, which are much more prominent between certain clusters (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is visible in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 where continuous regions connect distinct clusters.

claim: The amino acid compositions of LCRs that lie along bridges between clusters are continuous.
source: While cluster definitions are discrete, the amino acid compositions of the LCRs that lie along these bridges are continuous (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C where sequences along bridges show gradual compositional changes.

claim: Nuclear speckle proteins primarily populated a bridge between the R and S clusters in LCR sequence space.
source: Nuclear speckle proteins, which are commonly localized by LCRs known as RS-domains (Cáceres et al., 1997; Boucher et al., 2001), primarily populated a bridge between the R and S clusters in LCR sequence space (Figure 3B), and were significantly enriched in both of these amino acids (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and confirmed by statistical analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: Nuclear speckle protein LCRs were significantly enriched in R and S amino acids.
source: Nuclear speckle proteins, which are commonly localized by LCRs known as RS-domains (Cáceres et al., 1997; Boucher et al., 2001), primarily populated a bridge between the R and S clusters in LCR sequence space (Figure 3B), and were significantly enriched in both of these amino acids (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown through Wilcoxon rank sum tests in Figure 3E.

claim: LCRs of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins were heavily concentrated in a G/P-rich region.
source: LCRs of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins were heavily concentrated in a G/P-rich region (Figure 3C and F), reflecting the many, long collagen proteins in humans.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and confirmed by statistical analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: LCRs of nucleolar proteins largely mapped to the K-rich and E-rich clusters in LCR sequence space.
source: LCRs of nucleolar proteins largely mapped to the K-rich and E-rich clusters in LCR sequence space (Figure 3D and G), consistent with nucleolar localization signals possessing K-rich sequences (Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and confirmed by statistical analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: Nucleolar LCRs were significantly more likely than LCRs of speckle proteins to have a high frequency of E residues, but not D residues.
source: Nucleolar LCRs were significantly more likely than LCRs of speckle proteins to have a high frequency of E residues, but not D residues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown through statistical comparison in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The intrinsic disorder scores among K-enriched and E-enriched nucleolar LCRs are similar.
source: The intrinsic disorder scores (IUPred2) among these K- and E-enriched nucleolar LCRs are similar (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B comparing IUPred2 score distributions.

claim: E-enriched nucleolar LCRs exhibited a bimodal distribution of ANCHOR scores where one peak had much higher ANCHOR scores than K-enriched nucleolar LCRs.
source: However, while K-enriched nucleolar LCRs exhibited a unimodal distribution of ANCHOR scores (the probability of a disordered sequence to become ordered upon binding to a globular protein partner), E-enriched LCRs exhibited a bimodal distribution where one peak had much higher ANCHOR scores (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C comparing ANCHOR score distributions.

claim: TCOF contained the most E-enriched LCRs among nucleolar proteins with E-enriched LCRs.
source: Among proteins with E-enriched LCRs, we chose TCOF as a candidate scaffold because it contained the most E-enriched LCRs (Figure 4E) and was a multiple-mixed protein high in total LCRs but low in distinct LCRs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E as a histogram of E-enriched LCR counts.

claim: TCOF normally localizes to the nucleolus.
source: TCOF normally localizes to the nucleolus, as indicated by the nucleolar marker Fibrillarin and Hoechst-negative regions surrounded by heterochromatin (upper row in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TCOF ΔK forms assemblies similar in size and shape to WT TCOF.
source: When expressed in cells, TCOF ΔK forms assemblies similar in size and shape to WT TCOF (Figure 4F, green channel).
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 4F.

claim: TCOF ΔK was able to form assemblies outside of the nucleolus.
source: However, when assessed both by Fibrillarin costaining and heterochromatin-surrounded Hoechst-negative regions, TCOF ΔK was able to form assemblies outside of the nucleolus (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), showing that the region of TCOF containing its E-rich LCRs is sufficient for assembly.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The region of TCOF containing its E-rich LCRs is sufficient for assembly.
source: However, when assessed both by Fibrillarin costaining and heterochromatin-surrounded Hoechst-negative regions, TCOF ΔK was able to form assemblies outside of the nucleolus (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), showing that the region of TCOF containing its E-rich LCRs is sufficient for assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that TCOF ΔK, which lacks K-rich LCRs but retains E-rich LCRs, can still form assemblies.

claim: RPA1 and UBF1 colocalize with WT TCOF in the nucleolus.
source: Both RPA1 and UBF1 colocalize with WT TCOF in the nucleolus (upper row in Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RPA1 and UBF1 colocalize with TCOF ΔK assemblies outside the nucleolus.
source: When we assessed the localization of RPA1 and UBF1 in cells expressing TCOF ΔK, we observed that both of these proteins now colocalized with TCOF ΔK.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 4G.

claim: The enrichment of RPA1 in TCOF ΔK assemblies appears greater than enrichment of UBF1.
source: Moreover, the enrichment of RPA1, which contains two E-rich LCRs, in TCOF ΔK assemblies appears greater than enrichment of UBF1, which contains one E-rich LCR (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is observed through visual comparison of immunofluorescence in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A protein with many E-rich LCRs (TCOF) is a scaffold, and proteins with few E-rich LCRs (RPA1, UBF1) act as clients.
source: These results show that a protein with many E-rich LCRs (TCOF) is a scaffold, and that proteins with few E-rich LCRs act as clients (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing TCOF recruits RPA1 and UBF1.

claim: Some regions of sequence space were occupied to some degree by all species analyzed, while others appeared specific to certain species.
source: Some regions of sequence space were occupied to some degree by all species analyzed, while others appeared specific to certain species (Figure 5—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2–4 where species-specific occupancy patterns are visible.

claim: The space occupied by nucleolar LCRs from yeast and human were both common to the K-rich cluster as well as the E/D-rich clusters.
source: The space occupied by nucleolar LCRs from yeast and human were both common to the K-rich cluster as well as the E/D-rich clusters (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 6A, B), suggesting that the compositions of LCRs participating in the nucleolus are conserved across a large evolutionary distance, including the E-rich sequences discussed above (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 6A, B.

claim: The R/S-rich bridge between the R-rich and S-rich clusters was occupied by speckle annotations for both A. thaliana and H. sapiens.
source: Similarly, when comparing between speckle annotations for A. thaliana and H. sapiens, we found that the R/S-rich bridge between the R-rich and S-rich clusters was occupied for each (Figure 5—figure supplement 6C-F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6C-F.

claim: E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and A. thaliana had nearly no LCRs in the G/P cluster.
source: While E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and A. thaliana had nearly no LCRs in the G/P cluster, this cluster was much more occupied in metazoans (Figure 5C), corresponding with the emergence of collagens, a hallmark of the metazoan lineage (Hynes, 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C where the G/P cluster occupancy differs across species.

claim: The G/P cluster was much more occupied in metazoans than in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and A. thaliana.
source: While E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and A. thaliana had nearly no LCRs in the G/P cluster, this cluster was much more occupied in metazoans (Figure 5C), corresponding with the emergence of collagens, a hallmark of the metazoan lineage (Hynes, 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The gradual differences in occupancy of the G/P cluster between metazoan species correlated with the expansion of the extracellular matrix across metazoans.
source: The gradual differences in occupancy of the G/P cluster between the metazoan species (Figure 5C) correlated with the expansion of the extracellular matrix across metazoans (reviewed in Hynes, 2012), highlighting that the LCR map traces the progression of a higher order assembly across evolution.
evidence: This correlation is observed in Figure 5C and supported by citation to literature on ECM evolution.

claim: LCRs of cell wall proteins of A. thaliana primarily mapped to the P-rich cluster and a nearby P/S/Y-rich cluster.
source: LCRs of cell wall proteins of A. thaliana, for example, primarily mapped to the P-rich cluster and a nearby P/S/Y-rich cluster (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 6G), reflecting the set of hydroxyproline-rich cell wall proteins which include extensins, arabinogalactan proteins (AGPs) and proline-rich proteins (PRPs).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 6G.

claim: Extensins have SPPPP motifs and are important scaffolds for the assembly of the cell wall.
source: Extensins, which have SPPPP motifs, are known to be important scaffolds for the assembly of the cell wall, in which they are thought to form self-assembling networks to organize pectin (Cannon et al., 2008; Sede et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, LCRs of cell wall proteins mapped to the S-rich and T-rich clusters.
source: In S. cerevisiae, LCRs of cell wall proteins mapped to the S-rich and T-rich clusters (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 6H), which included flocculation proteins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 6H.

claim: S- and T-rich LCRs in S. cerevisiae cell wall proteins are often sites for O-mannosylation in mannoproteins, which is crucial for the integrity of the cell wall.
source: These S- and T-rich LCRs are often sites for O-mannosylation in mannoproteins, which is crucial for the integrity of the cell wall (Gentzsch and Tanner, 1996; González et al., 2012; Neubert et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When a given assembly is conserved, occupancy of the corresponding LCR sequence space is also conserved.
source: Firstly, we show that when a given assembly is conserved, occupancy of the corresponding LCR sequence space is also conserved.
evidence: This is demonstrated through examples like nucleolar and speckle proteins showing similar sequence space occupancy across species.

claim: The emergence of a higher order assembly can correspond to the population of a previously unoccupied sequence space.
source: Secondly, the emergence of a higher order assembly can correspond to the population of a previously unoccupied sequence space.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the G/P cluster being populated in metazoans but not in earlier-diverging species.

claim: Higher order assemblies with different physical properties occupy different regions of sequence space, even when they fulfill similar roles in their respective species.
source: Finally, higher order assemblies with different physical properties occupy different regions of sequence space, even when they fulfill similar roles in their respective species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by plant and yeast cell walls occupying different regions of sequence space despite both being extracellular assemblies.

claim: The T/H-rich cluster is specific to D. rerio among the species analyzed in the main cross-species comparison.
source: Upon comparing sequence space occupancy between species, we found various species-specific regions which lacked detailed annotations, one of which was the T/H-rich cluster specific to D. rerio (Figure 6A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Many of the LCRs in the T/H-rich cluster included direct TH repeats.
source: Many of the LCRs in this cluster included direct TH repeats (Figure 6A), which was of particular interest because these amino acid residues may facilitate assembly via several mechanisms, including polar interactions through threonine or cation-pi interactions of histidine.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A where example sequences are displayed.

claim: The T/H-rich cluster contained 97 proteins with T/H-rich LCRs.
source: Therefore, we decided to further investigate this T/H-rich cluster, which contained 97 proteins with T/H-rich LCRs.
evidence: This is a direct count from the analysis.

claim: Protein A0A0G2KXX0 had 17 total LCRs and only three distinct LCR types, of which 15 were T/H-rich LCRs.
source: For example, in the plot of total vs. distinct LCRs for the T/H-rich cluster, protein A0A0G2KXX0 had 17 total LCRs and only three distinct LCR types. Of these, 15 were T/H-rich LCRs, with only 1 LCR in each of the other distinct types (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through the dotplot and LCR analysis.

claim: All teleost fish analyzed (zebrafish, electric eel, northern pike, Atlantic salmon, Japanese pufferfish) substantially occupied the T/H-rich cluster.
source: Of these fishes, all but the spotted gar substantially occupied the T/H-rich cluster.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D where teleost fish show high occupancy of the T/H cluster.

claim: The spotted gar was only lightly occupied in the T/H-rich cluster with 14 LCRs.
source: The fishes which heavily occupied the T/H-rich cluster each contained ~200 T/H LCRs, while the spotted gar was only lightly occupied with 14 LCRs (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The difference in T/H cluster occupancy between teleost fish and spotted gar correlated with evolutionary relationships, with teleosts having high occupancy and holosteans (spotted gar) having low occupancy.
source: However, this difference in occupancy of the T/H cluster correlated exactly with evolutionary relationships between these fishes. Those containing T/H-rich LCRs belonged to Teleostei, while the spotted gar, which did not, belonged to Holostei, a group which diverged from Teleostei in Actinopterygii.
evidence: This correlation is observed in Figure 6D where phylogenetic relationships match T/H cluster occupancy patterns.

claim: The seven species analyzed outside of Actinopterygii had a very low number of T/H-rich LCRs.
source: Moreover, the seven species we analyzed outside of Actinopterygii had a very low number of T/H-rich LCRs as well (Figure 6A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which strongly suggests that T/H-rich LCRs are teleost specific and may form a conserved higher order assembly in these species.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: T/H-rich LCRs are teleost specific and may form a conserved higher order assembly in these species.
source: Moreover, the seven species we analyzed outside of Actinopterygii had a very low number of T/H-rich LCRs as well (Figure 6A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which strongly suggests that T/H-rich LCRs are teleost specific and may form a conserved higher order assembly in these species.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic specificity and the presence of scaffold-like proteins with many T/H-rich LCRs.

claim: Natural LCRs distribute across a continuum of sequence space.
source: In our LCR map, we find that natural LCRs distribute across a continuum of sequence space.
evidence: This is shown in the UMAP visualizations where LCRs form continuous distributions rather than discrete groups.

claim: The inhibitory activity of the acidic LCR in G3BP1 is independent of the primary sequence of the acidic LCR.
source: This inhibitory activity of the acidic LCR is independent of the primary sequence of the acidic LCR, and is abolished by substitution of negatively charged glutamic acid for neutral glutamine residues (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CK2 binds and phosphorylates serines in acidic contexts.
source: One well understood kinase, CK2, binds and phosphorylates serines in acidic contexts (Rusin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TCOF has been shown to be regulated by CK2.
source: Notably, TCOF, which has many E-rich LCRs in the bridge between S and E, has been shown to be regulated by CK2 (Werner et al., 2015; Werner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The physical properties of R and K substantially differ, while the difference between D and E is much more subtle.
source: In fact, recent evidence showed that the physical properties of R and K substantially differ, while the difference between D and E is much more subtle (Wang et al., 2018; Greig et al., 2020; Fossat et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The G-P-P motif-containing LCRs in various collagens form key assemblies in the ECM.
source: The K-rich LCRs of nucleolar proteins such as RPA43 are required for their higher order assembly and integration into the nucleolus, while the G-P-P motif-containing LCRs in various collagens form key assemblies in the ECM (Timpl et al., 1981; Mould and Hulmes, 1987; Hansen and Bruckner, 2003) and the G/V/P-rich LCRs of elastin assemble to provide ECM elasticity (Urry et al., 1974; Rauscher et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The G/V/P-rich LCRs of elastin assemble to provide ECM elasticity.
source: The K-rich LCRs of nucleolar proteins such as RPA43 are required for their higher order assembly and integration into the nucleolus, while the G-P-P motif-containing LCRs in various collagens form key assemblies in the ECM (Timpl et al., 1981; Mould and Hulmes, 1987; Hansen and Bruckner, 2003) and the G/V/P-rich LCRs of elastin assemble to provide ECM elasticity (Urry et al., 1974; Rauscher et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of glycines in ECM collagen proteins is crucial for tight packing of helices to form the collagen triple helix.
source: LCRs of ECM proteins occupy the G/P-rich cluster and the presence of glycines in ECM collagen proteins is crucial for tight packing of helices to form the collagen triple helix (Beck et al., 2000), which is the basis for higher order assembly of most of the tissues in the human body.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The collagen triple helix is the basis for higher order assembly of most of the tissues in the human body.
source: LCRs of ECM proteins occupy the G/P-rich cluster and the presence of glycines in ECM collagen proteins is crucial for tight packing of helices to form the collagen triple helix (Beck et al., 2000), which is the basis for higher order assembly of most of the tissues in the human body.
evidence: This is supported by citation and general biological knowledge about collagen's role in tissues.
